messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 57

At 48, she still talks about the accident as if it happened in the next room rather than years ago, something that is never fully behind her. She is a North American woman who has built much of her life around service, and before the accident she moves through her days with the steady practicality of someone used to helping other people carry what is heavy. As a social ministry worker, she spends her time visiting people in crisis, organizing meals, arranging shelter, and showing up in places where hope is often thin. She has always been the one who keeps going, the one who can sit with pain without flinching. That is part of what makes the accident feel, to her, like a betrayal of her own body and expectations.

The traumatic event happens on an ordinary day, which is one of the reasons it stays so lodged in her mind. She is traveling for work when her vehicle is struck in a life-threatening collision. In the moments before impact, she remembers only the ordinary details—the feel of the steering wheel, the road ahead, the thought of where she needs to be next. Then there is the violent sound, the wrenching force, the sudden loss of control. She believes she is going to die. Time seems to break apart. She is aware of metal crumpling, of her own breathing becoming sharp and shallow, of a smell she later describes as “burning and strange.” Her body is flooded with panic, but there is also an eerie stillness, a sense that her mind is watching from somewhere outside the wreck.

In the days that follow, she is physically injured and shaken in a way she has difficulty putting into words. Friends and coworkers expect gratitude that she survived, and she gives it, but inside she feels disoriented and brittle. Sleep does not come easily. When she does sleep, she wakes abruptly, heart pounding, with the impact replaying in vivid fragments. She begins to avoid the route where it happened and, later, any highway that resembles it. At first she tells herself this is sensible caution. Then she notices how quickly her body reacts—tight chest, ringing in her ears, hands damp at the wheel—whenever she gets into a car. She becomes vigilant in a way that feels exhausting, scanning the road, the mirrors, the movements of other drivers, unable to relax even on quiet streets.

Over time, she starts to feel less like herself. She remains committed to her work, but the job now takes more effort. She finds herself arriving earlier to appointments so she can choose the parking space closest to the door. She checks exits automatically in unfamiliar buildings. If she hears a sudden bang—someone dropping a file box, a door slamming—her whole body jerks with a wave of panic that is humiliating in its intensity. She hates the way her fear intrudes into places that matter to her, especially the shelters and community kitchens where she once felt most useful and grounded. She worries that others will notice how tense she is, how often she is forcing herself not to flinch.

She also struggles with the emotional aftermath in quieter, less visible ways. There are moments when she feels numb, almost sealed off, as if the accident has cut her from the easy warmth she used to feel with people. At other times she becomes unexpectedly irritable or tearful, then embarrassed by the intensity of her reaction. She thinks often about how easily everything could have ended and feels a persistent, unshakable sense of vulnerability. Driving is no longer routine but a negotiation with dread. On difficult days, she rehearses what she would do if another collision happened, as though preparation might prevent catastrophe. She knows this does not make her safer, but she cannot seem to stop.

Being single means there is no partner at home to notice the full extent of what she is carrying, and she is used to being the one who does not ask for much. So she keeps going, meets her responsibilities, answers her phone, and shows up for others even when she feels frayed and exhausted. Yet there is a private grief in her now: grief for the ease she once had in the world, for the assumption that roads, crossings, and ordinary errands were safe enough to take for granted. She is still devoted to her ministry work, still compassionate and competent, but she moves through life with an alertness that never quite rests, as if part of her is still listening for the sound of impact.
